case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, under the Tobacco Control Act’s judicial-review and venue provisions, e-cigarette retailers/distributors may rely on their own alleged injury to secure Fifth Circuit venue to challenge FDA’s denial of a manufacturer’s premarket tobacco product applications (PMTAs), even though the denial order is directed to the manufacturer and retailers had no legal right to sell the products before or after the denial.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act (TCA), particularly 21 U.S.C. § 387l(a)(1) (judicial review; who may seek review and where), and related TCA provisions bearing on who may challenge other types of FDA tobacco orders (including 21 U.S.C. § 387j(d)(2)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The FDA argues that the Fifth Circuit is allowing an impermissible 'mix-and-match' theory of venue and standing under 21 U.S.C. § 387l(a)(1): retailers/distributors cannot create proper venue by joining a petition for review of a manufacturer-directed PMTA denial because the denial order does not change the retailers’ legal rights or duties (they lacked legal authority to sell the unauthorized products both before and after the denial). Any claimed harm is at most a change in expectations about FDA enforcement priorities, which the FDA says is not a cognizable 'adverse effect' under the statute and would intrude on the Executive’s Article II enforcement discretion. The FDA also emphasizes that the Fifth Circuit’s approach effectively nullifies Congress’s venue limits by enabling forum shopping—especially after the Fifth Circuit’s earlier venue ruling in related litigation (referenced as Wages/R.J. Reynolds Vapor Co.), which has prompted out-of-circuit manufacturers to file in the Fifth Circuit.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Reynolds and the aligned retail/distributor petitioners contend that § 387l(a)(1) authorizes review by 'any person adversely affected' and that retailers/distributors are adversely affected in fact and in business reality because the denial order cuts off the ability to sell the products and threatens store closure and lost revenue (as reflected in declarations such as Avail Vapor Texas stating the store would close without access to Vuse products). They argue that this satisfies the statute’s standing/eligibility to seek review and, given the Fifth Circuit’s prior published decision holding venue proper in similar circumstances, stare decisis controls. They further argue that the FDA’s reliance on other TCA provisions (e.g., § 387j(d)(2) concerning who may challenge a marketing withdrawal order) is inapposite to PMTA denial orders and does not override the broad 'any person adversely affected' language for denials.
key_precedents: National Ass’n of Manufacturers v. Department of Defense, 583 U.S. 109 (2018)
City of Ocala v. Rojas, 143 S. Ct. 764 (2023) (Gorsuch, J., statement respecting denial of certiorari)
R.J. Reynolds Vapor Co. (Fifth Circuit decision referenced in the record as 65 F.4th 182 (5th Cir. 2023))

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains the breadth of “any person adversely affected,” but—consistent with Justice Kagan’s structural account—the phrase must be read in tandem with the order-centered review-and-venue scheme, which targets parties whose legal rights or duties are altered by the FDA order. A PMTA denial is directed to the applicant and leaves retailers without any lawful entitlement to sell the unapproved product both before and after, so the retailers’ asserted injury is an indirect economic effect rather than the statutorily relevant “adverse” change. Justice Barrett’s reliance on O’Bannon helps draw an administrable line between direct legal regulation and downstream commercial ripple effects, and Justice Gorsuch is right that allowing retailer joinder would invite venue laundering and forum shopping that would effectively defeat Congress’s calibrated venue choice. National Ass’n of Manufacturers reinforces that “any” cannot be used to dissolve the limiting phrase that follows, supporting a narrow holding that retailers may not invoke § 387l(a)(1) to set venue for manufacturer-directed PMTA denials.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Respondent’s strongest point remains the breadth of “any person adversely affected,” which in isolation might reach downstream economic injury, but text in context matters: as Chief Justice Roberts explains, National Ass’n of Manufacturers confirms that “any” cannot erase the limiting phrase that follows, and here “adversely affected” is best read to require a legally operative change worked by the FDA “order.” A PMTA denial is an order directed to the applicant/manufacturer and does not alter a retailer’s legal rights or duties; as Justice Barrett’s O’Bannon analogy underscores, incidental economic fallout from a decision regulating someone else is not the sort of adverse effect Congress used to trigger this specialized review-and-venue regime. Justice Gorsuch and Justice Alito rightly add that treating shifted enforcement expectations as cognizable adverse effect risks the separation-of-powers concerns highlighted in United States v. Texas and would invite forum-shopping that defeats Congress’s calibrated venue scheme. None of these counterarguments undermines the original public meaning of § 387l(a)(1) as tethered to the order’s direct legal consequences, so I remain with Petitioner.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Respondents’ strongest point remains the breadth of “any person adversely affected,” which in isolation could sweep in retailers with economic loss. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes via National Ass’n of Manufacturers, “any” does not nullify the limiting phrase that follows; in context of this specialized review-and-venue scheme, the relevant “adverse effect” must be tied to the legal operation of the FDA “order,” not merely downstream commercial consequences. Justice Barrett’s reliance on O’Bannon reinforces the administrable line that incidental economic fallout from an order directed to another is generally insufficient when the statute is keyed to the order’s direct legal effect; here retailers had no legal entitlement to sell an unauthorized product both before and after the PMTA denial. And as Justice Gorsuch notes, treating shifted enforcement expectations as “adverse effect” would risk the separation-of-powers concern flagged in United States v. Texas and would predictably invite venue manipulation and forum shopping, undermining Congress’s calibrated scheme.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondents’ strongest point remains the plain-language breadth of “any person adversely affected,” because retailers can face immediate economic losses when a PMTA is denied. But as Chief Justice Roberts persuasively explains using National Ass’n of Manufacturers, “any” cannot be read to erase the statute’s order-centered limitation, and here the FDA order legally operates on the applicant’s PMTA—not on retailers whose legal entitlement to sell an unauthorized product is the same before and after. Justice Barrett’s O’Bannon analogy reinforces a pragmatic, administrable line: downstream economic disappointment from a decision directed at another is not the kind of adverse legal effect Congress likely meant to trigger this specialized review-and-venue mechanism, especially given the forum-shopping risks. I also agree with Justice Gorsuch that treating shifted enforcement expectations as a cognizable adverse effect would pull courts toward supervising enforcement discretion in tension with United States v. Texas, with especially uneven consequences for uniformity and access to justice across circuits.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondents’ strongest point remains the apparent breadth of “any person adversely affected” in § 387l(a)(1), which could linguistically sweep in retailers who lose sales after a PMTA denial. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes via National Ass’n of Manufacturers, “any” cannot be read to nullify the operative limitation that the petitioner be adversely affected in the way the review-and-venue scheme is designed to capture—i.e., by the order’s direct legal consequences. Justice Barrett’s O’Bannon analogy is persuasive on administrability: collateral economic ripple effects from an order directed at someone else are not the kind of order-linked adverse change Congress typically uses to trigger special review and venue rules, and allowing retailer joinder would predictably enable forum shopping that makes the statute’s venue calibration incoherent. Nothing in United States v. Texas cuts against that order-centered reading; if anything, treating shifted enforcement expectations as cognizable “adverse effects” would exacerbate the Article II concerns Roberts and Alito identify.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondents’ best textual point—that “any person adversely affected” can naturally reach economically harmed retailers—still fails once we read the phrase in full statutory context: the “adverse effect” must be tied to the legal operation of the specific FDA “order,” not merely its downstream market consequences. As Chief Justice Roberts explains relying on National Ass’n of Manufacturers, “any” cannot be used to erase the limiting language that follows, and § 387l(a)(1)’s venue calibration (residence/principal place of business) makes little sense if non-addressees can manufacture preferred-circuit venue through joinder. Justice Barrett’s O’Bannon analogy underscores the administrable distinction between direct alteration of legal rights/duties and incidental economic fallout from a decision aimed at someone else; here retailers had no lawful entitlement to sell an unauthorized product either before or after the PMTA denial. Finally, United States v. Texas, as several colleagues note, cautions against transforming disappointed enforcement expectations into a judicially cognizable “adverse effect” that would invite courts to supervise Executive enforcement discretion and destabilize separation of powers.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondents’ best argument—that retailers are “adversely affected” economically and thus qualify as “any person” under § 387l(a)(1)—has surface plausibility, but it fails once the phrase is read in its order-centered context. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, National Ass’n of Manufacturers confirms that “any” cannot dissolve the limiting requirement that the petitioner be adversely affected in the legally relevant way contemplated by this specialized review-and-venue provision; here, the PMTA denial alters the manufacturer’s legal position, not the retailer’s, who lacked lawful authority to sell the product both before and after. Justice Barrett’s O’Bannon analogy further persuades me that downstream commercial disappointment from a decision directed at another party is not the kind of cognizable adverse effect Congress typically uses to trigger a tailored review/venue regime. On an institutional and practical level, recognizing retailer standing here would predictably enable venue manufacturing and forum shopping that would undercut Congress’s calibrated venue choice and the Court’s interest in administrable, legitimacy-protecting rules.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondents’ strongest point remains the breadth of “any person adversely affected,” which in isolation could encompass retailers’ economic injury; but in context § 387l(a)(1) is an order-centered review-and-venue provision, and the relevant “adverse” effect must be tied to the legal operation of the FDA “order,” not downstream commercial disappointment. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on National Ass’n of Manufacturers persuasively shows that “any” cannot be used to enlarge the limiting phrase that follows in a specialized review/venue scheme, and Justice Kagan is right that a PMTA denial changes the applicant’s legal posture while retailers’ legal status (no lawful entitlement to sell an unauthorized product) is the same before and after. My analogy to O’Bannon continues to fit: collateral economic fallout from government action directed at another party is ordinarily insufficient when Congress keys review rights to the direct legal effects of an order. Allowing retailer joinder to set venue would effectively defeat Congress’s calibrated venue limits and, as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Alito note, risks converting enforcement-expectations harms into review-triggering injuries in tension with United States v. Texas.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondents’ strongest point remains the plain-language breadth of “any person adversely affected,” which in isolation could reach retailers with real economic losses, but that reading is undercut by the statute’s order-centered design and Congress’s calibrated venue scheme. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on National Ass’n of Manufacturers appropriately cabins “any” so it cannot erase the limiting phrase that follows; here, the relevant “adverse effect” must be legally tethered to the FDA order, and a PMTA denial changes the applicant’s legal posture without altering retailers’ baseline lack of authorization to sell the unapproved product. Justice Barrett’s O’Bannon analogy helps draw an administrable line between direct legal regulation and downstream commercial disappointment, and I share Justice Kagan’s concern that allowing retailer-driven petitions would predictably enable venue manipulation and undermine procedural fairness and uniformity. United States v. Texas, as Justice Gorsuch notes, reinforces that we should be wary of treating shifted enforcement expectations as a cognizable adverse effect that expands judicial supervision in a way Congress did not clearly authorize.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 387l(a)(1) permits review by “any person adversely affected,” but, as National Ass’n of Manufacturers v. Department of Defense explains, “any” cannot expand the limiting phrase that follows, and the TCA’s structure ties review and venue to those whose legal rights or duties are altered by the challenged FDA order. A PMTA denial is directed to the manufacturer and does not change retailers’ legal authority, because they had no right to sell an unauthorized product before or after the denial; their asserted harm is derivative and, at most, a shifted expectation about enforcement, which this Court has cautioned against treating as a cognizable basis for judicial review in ways that intrude on Article II enforcement discretion (see United States v. Texas). Allowing retailers to supply venue would effectively nullify Congress’s venue limits in § 387l(a)(1) by enabling forum shopping, contrary to the Court’s insistence on respecting carefully drawn judicial-review and venue provisions (National Ass’n of Manufacturers). A narrow ruling for FDA best preserves the statute’s design and institutional legitimacy by preventing “mix-and-match” standing/venue strategies while leaving manufacturers—the parties directly regulated—to pursue review in the proper venue.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text and structure of the TCA indicate that judicial review under 21 U.S.C. § 387l(a)(1) attaches to the persons whose legal rights or duties are altered by the FDA order, and a PMTA denial is directed to the manufacturer’s application rather than imposing any new legal disability on downstream retailers who lacked lawful authority to market an unapproved product both before and after the denial. Reading “any person adversely affected” to permit retailers to supply venue and standing for a manufacturer-directed order would stretch the statutory phrase beyond its ordinary meaning and effectively defeat Congress’s venue limits—an approach this Court has rejected when construing specialized judicial-review and venue provisions. National Ass’n of Manufacturers v. Department of Defense confirms that “any” does not expand the limiting phrase that follows and counsels against interpretations that enable forum shopping through venue-expanding constructions. The Act’s detailed, differentiated review mechanisms for different kinds of tobacco orders (including the more specific review provisions in 21 U.S.C. § 387j(d)(2)) reinforce that Congress did not silently authorize the retailer “mix-and-match” theory here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 387l(a)(1) permits review by a “person adversely affected,” but the denial order at issue is directed to the manufacturer and does not alter retailers’ legal rights or duties because they had no lawful entitlement to sell unauthorized products either before or after the denial. Reading “any person” to allow retailers to supply venue for a manufacturer’s challenge would impermissibly expand Congress’s carefully drawn review-and-venue scheme and invite forum shopping, contrary to National Ass’n of Manufacturers v. Department of Defense, 583 U.S. 109 (2018) (the word “any” cannot expand the limiting phrase that follows). The TCA’s structure—including provisions like § 387j(d)(2) specifying who may challenge other tobacco orders—supports a contextual, order-specific approach rather than a “mix-and-match” theory that would effectively nullify venue limits. Allowing venue based on retailers’ alleged injury here would also risk converting shifting enforcement expectations into a cognizable “adverse effect,” intruding on Executive enforcement discretion in tension with United States v. Texas, 599 U.S. 670 (2023).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 387l(a)(1) allows review by “any person adversely affected,” but the Tobacco Control Act’s structure ties reviewability and venue to the kind of order at issue and the party whose legal interests the order changes; retailers here had no legal right to market the products either before or after the manufacturer’s PMTA denial, so their asserted business harms do not supply the statute’s requisite “adverse effect” for purposes of venue. Reading “any” to permit retailer joinder to manufacture Fifth Circuit venue would defeat Congress’s evident venue limits and invite forum shopping, contrary to this Court’s approach to judicial-review/venue provisions in National Ass’n of Manufacturers v. Department of Defense, 583 U.S. 109 (2018) (the word “any” cannot expand the operative limits that follow). The Act’s more targeted review provisions elsewhere (e.g., § 387j(d)(2)’s specification of who may challenge certain marketing orders) reinforce that Congress did not mean to allow a free-floating, business-injury-based route to venue untethered to the order’s legal effect on the petitioner. A narrower reading is also more workable and avoids entangling courts in challenges premised on shifts in expected enforcement rather than changed legal rights.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 387l(a)(1) permits a petition only by a person “adversely affected” by the “order” and ties venue to that petitioner’s residence or principal place of business; here the PMTA denial order runs to the manufacturer, while retailers had no legal entitlement to market the products either before or after the denial, so any claimed injury is at most an enforcement-expectations or economic ripple effect rather than a change in legal rights or duties cognizable under the Act. Reading “any person” to allow downstream sellers to create venue would improperly expand the venue provision beyond its textual limits and invite forum shopping—an approach this Court rejected when construing similar judicial-review venue provisions in National Ass’n of Manufacturers v. Department of Defense, 583 U.S. 109 (2018) (the word “any” cannot expand the phrase that follows). The Act’s structure reinforces the point: Congress specified who may seek review for other FDA tobacco orders (e.g., 21 U.S.C. § 387j(d)(2)), suggesting it did not silently authorize collateral review by non-addressees for PMTA denials. Allowing such petitions would also pressure Article II enforcement discretion by turning generalized downstream business effects into a statutory right to sue, contrary to the separation-of-powers concerns reflected in cases like United States v. Texas, 599 U.S. 670 (2023).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 387l(a)(1) permits petitions by a “person adversely affected” and fixes venue accordingly, but the PMTA denial order is directed to the manufacturer and does not alter retailers’ legal rights or duties, given that retailers had no lawful entitlement to sell unauthorized products either before or after the denial. Reading “any person adversely affected” to allow retailers to manufacture venue would be an impermissible venue-expanding construction that invites forum shopping, contrary to Congress’s evident choice to limit where these challenges may be brought and our caution against such readings in National Ass’n of Manufacturers v. Department of Defense, 583 U.S. 109 (2018) (the word “any” cannot expand the limiting phrase that follows). The TCA’s structure reinforces that Congress speaks specifically when it wants to broaden who may seek review of particular tobacco orders (cf. 21 U.S.C. § 387j(d)(2)), supporting a restrained interpretation that ties review/venue to the party whose legal interests are directly regulated by the order. Practical workability and institutional concerns also favor rejecting a “mix-and-match” standing/venue theory that would undermine uniform administration of the TCA and encourage strategic filings in a preferred circuit.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 387l(a)(1) authorizes petitions by “any person adversely affected” and fixes venue by the petitioner’s residence or principal place of business, but the text and structure of the TCA indicate that a downstream commercial disappointment from an order directed to someone else is not the kind of “adverse effect” Congress meant to trigger this special review-and-venue regime. Retailers/distributors had no legal entitlement to market the products before the PMTA denial and none after; their asserted injury is thus not tied to any change in their own legal rights or duties, resembling the indirect, third-party effect this Court has treated as insufficient in analogous contexts (O’Bannon v. Town Court Nursing Center, 447 U.S. 773, 788 (1980)). Reading “any” to sweep in such indirect injuries would “expand the phrase that follows” and effectively nullify Congress’s venue limits by permitting forum shopping, contrary to National Ass’n of Manufacturers v. Department of Defense, 583 U.S. 109 (2018), which emphasizes close adherence to statutory review/venue text and rejects interpretations that enlarge special review provisions beyond their terms. Given the TCA’s differentiated treatment of who may challenge different FDA tobacco actions (including § 387j(d)(2)), the better textual reading is that § 387l(a)(1) does not allow retailers to bootstrap venue for a manufacturer-directed PMTA denial based solely on their own asserted economic harms.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 387l(a)(1) permits review by an “any person adversely affected,” but the relevant “adverse effect” must be tied to a legal change worked by the FDA order and to Congress’s calibrated judicial-review/venue scheme; retailers who lacked any legal right to market unauthorized products before or after a PMTA denial do not become proper challengers/venue-creators simply by alleging downstream economic harm. The TCA’s structure—especially the way Congress elsewhere specifies who may seek review of other tobacco orders, see 21 U.S.C. § 387j(d)(2)—supports reading PMTA-denial review as centered on the applicant/manufacturer rather than enabling “mix-and-match” standing/venue that invites forum shopping. National Ass’n of Manufacturers v. Department of Defense, 583 U.S. 109 (2018), reinforces that broad words like “any” do not override the limits Congress built into specialized review and venue provisions, and allowing retailers to manufacture Fifth Circuit venue would undermine those limits with significant practical consequences for uniform administration of federal law. Procedural fairness and administrability favor a clear rule: venue follows the party whose legal rights and obligations are directly determined by the order being reviewed.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, under the Tobacco Control Act’s judicial-review and venue provisions, e-cigarette retailers/distributors can establish statutory standing and venue in a circuit by joining a manufacturer’s petition for review of an FDA marketing-denial order, even though the denial order is directed to the manufacturer’s premarket tobacco product applications.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act (TCA), including 21 U.S.C. § 387l(a)(1) (judicial review; “any person adversely affected” and venue language) and related provisions such as 21 U.S.C. § 387j(d)(2) (marketing withdrawal orders; review by “holder of [the] application”); also implicated are Article II enforcement-discretion principles (as discussed via precedent).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: FDA argues the Fifth Circuit’s venue theory improperly allows a “mix-and-match” approach in which a retailer/distributor’s residence is used to create venue for a manufacturer’s challenge. In FDA’s view, a marketing-denial order does not ‘adversely affect’ retailers in a legally cognizable way because retailers had no lawful right to sell the unauthorized products before the denial and still have no such right after it—so their legal position is unchanged. At most, the denial alters FDA’s enforcement priorities or the likelihood of enforcement, which FDA contends is not an ‘adverse effect’ for purposes of statutory standing/venue and would intrude on the Executive’s Article II discretion to prioritize enforcement. FDA also contends this interpretation is required by the structure and purpose of the TCA’s venue limits, which would be undermined if manufacturers could forum-shop by adding downstream sellers in favorable circuits.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Reynolds and the joined retailers/distributors argue venue is proper in the Fifth Circuit under circuit precedent (including R.J. Reynolds Vapor Co., 65 F.4th 182) because the retailers/distributors are ‘persons adversely affected’ by FDA’s denial orders: the denial threatens their ability to continue operating (e.g., a retailer declaration that losing authorization to sell Vuse products would force store closure and cessation of business). They contend the TCA’s judicial-review provision grants broad standing to ‘any person adversely affected’ by FDA decisions, and that FDA’s objections (including that products were allegedly unlawful to sell absent approval and that only application-holders can seek review in other contexts like withdrawal orders) do not negate standing/venue for denial-order challenges. They further rely on stare decisis in the Fifth Circuit, emphasizing the court has already upheld venue on materially similar facts and that FDA either previously lost or failed to properly raise these statutory arguments earlier.
key_precedents: R.J. Reynolds Vapor Co. v. FDA, 65 F.4th 182 (5th Cir. 2023)
National Ass’n of Manufacturers v. Department of Defense, 583 U.S. 109 (2018)
City of Ocala v. Rojas, 143 S. Ct. 764 (2023) (Gorsuch, J., respecting denial of certiorari)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that we must take seriously Congress’s choice of “any person adversely affected” in § 387l(a)(1) and its contrasting “holder of an application” language in § 387j(d)(2); we cannot simply read “any” out of the statute. But, as Justice Kagan and Justice Alito emphasize, the limiting work is done by “adversely affected” when read in context of an application-centered marketing-denial order and a venue provision keyed to the petitioner’s residence—otherwise downstream sellers can supply a preferred forum through strategic joinder, effectively nullifying Congress’s channeling choice. National Ass’n of Manufacturers supports enforcing Congress’s channeling/venue architecture rather than letting broad prefatory words swallow the limiting phrases that follow, and United States v. Texas reinforces the caution against treating shifts in enforcement risk and derivative economic fallout as the kind of statutory adverse effect that opens the courthouse doors in this posture. I therefore adhere to a narrow holding: these retailers’ asserted harms are too indirect to anchor § 387l(a)(1) venue for review of an order directed to the PMTA applicant.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s venue-manufacture concern is a policy objection that cannot justify rewriting § 387l(a)(1)’s capacious text—“any person adversely affected”—or ignoring Congress’s deliberate choice to peg venue to the petitioner’s residence or principal place of business. Justice Alito’s reliance on United States v. Texas does not move me because the injury here flows from a final agency order that changes the legal status of products in commerce and predictably constrains retailers’ lawful business, not merely from a generalized shift in enforcement priorities. Nor does National Ass’n of Manufacturers support narrowing “any person” to “application holder”; it cautions against expanding review beyond statutory limits, and the limit colleagues propose would be judicially implied, not textually grounded. Congress demonstrated in § 387j(d)(2) that it knew how to confine review to an “application holder,” and we should not supply that limitation where Congress omitted it.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to press the breadth of “any person adversely affected” and to note that Congress elsewhere used “holder” when it wanted to, but that does not resolve what counts as being “adversely affected” by this particular kind of application-directed order in this particular statutory scheme. As the Chief Justice explains, if downstream retailers with only derivative economic harm can always qualify, the residence/principal-place-of-business venue clause becomes a party-controlled device for “mix-and-match” forum shopping, effectively nullifying Congress’s channeling choice—something National Ass’n of Manufacturers cautions us not to do by letting a broad word (“any”) swallow the limiting work done by the rest of the provision. I also remain skeptical, consistent with United States v. Texas, of treating shifts in enforcement risk and economic fallout (without a change in a lawful entitlement) as the kind of statutorily cognizable adverse effect that can anchor venue for reviewing an order addressed to the PMTA applicant. On a textualist reading attentive to statutory context and practical consequences, retailers here are not the relevant “adversely affected” petitioners for purposes of manufacturing venue.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to press the breadth of “any person adversely affected,” and the contrast with § 387j(d)(2)’s “holder” language means we cannot smuggle in a holder-only rule by fiat. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan that “adversely affected” must be read in context of what the marketing-denial order does as law: it operates on the applicant’s authorization status, while retailers’ harm is downstream economic fallout and increased enforcement exposure rather than a new legal disability imposed on them by the order itself. National Ass’n of Manufacturers matters here because it warns against letting broad terms defeat Congress’s channeling/venue design; allowing retailer joinder to anchor venue would invite precisely the “mix-and-match” forum selection Congress’s exclusive-review scheme is meant to prevent. And as Justice Alito notes via United States v. Texas, treating shifts in enforcement risk as the key to courthouse access risks pulling courts toward supervising enforcement discretion in a way that is especially harmful to administrability and, pragmatically, to vulnerable communities who bear the costs of unstable regulatory regimes.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that “any person adversely affected” is facially broad and that Congress elsewhere used “holder” when it meant to be specific, but that does not resolve what counts as being “adversely affected” by an MDO within this particular, application-centered review scheme. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, reading “any” to let downstream retailers join solely to anchor venue would functionally nullify § 387l(a)(1)’s venue-channeling design and invite the very mix-and-match forum shopping Congress ordinarily prevents in exclusive-review provisions—a structural incoherence National Ass’n of Manufacturers cautions against when broad words are followed by limiting machinery. United States v. Texas, invoked by Justice Alito, reinforces the administrability concern: treating downstream economic fallout and enforcement-risk shifts as the relevant “adverse effect” would turn enforcement posture into a ticket to court in preferred circuits, destabilizing the scheme. On my pragmatic textualism, the best reading is that “adversely affected” here is tethered to the legal effect of the order on its regulated addressee (the applicant), not derivative commercial consequences that do not change the retailer’s statutory entitlement to market an unauthorized product.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to press the breadth of “any person adversely affected” and to note Congress’s ability to say “holder” elsewhere, but that does not resolve what counts as being “adversely affected” by this particular agency action in this statutory setting. As the Chief Justice emphasizes, § 387l(a)(1)’s venue clause is part of a channeling scheme, and reading “any” to allow downstream sellers to join chiefly to supply a favored forum would let parties nullify Congress’s venue design—exactly the kind of move we rejected in National Ass’n of Manufacturers, where “any” could not be used to overwhelm limiting language and channeling structure. United States v. Texas reinforces my reluctance to treat increased enforcement risk and derivative economic fallout—where the order is directed to the PMTA applicant and retailers lacked a lawful entitlement to sell unauthorized products anyway—as the sort of statutorily cognizable “adverse effect” that opens the courthouse doors in a way that invites judicial management of executive enforcement. So I remain with petitioner on a narrow, context-sensitive reading that preserves the statute’s application-centered review and venue framework.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that “any person adversely affected” is broad and that Congress used “holder” in § 387j(d)(2), but that does not resolve what counts as an “adverse effect” in this application-centered review scheme and how that term interacts with Congress’s venue channeling. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, if downstream retailers’ derivative economic harms (or enforcement-risk shifts) suffice, then manufacturers can manufacture venue by joinder, effectively nullifying the residence/principal-place-of-business limitation that Congress put in § 387l(a)(1). National Ass’n of Manufacturers supports giving full effect to Congress’s channeling choices and the limiting function of the words that follow “any,” rather than letting a broad opening word swallow the venue structure. Justice Alito’s U.S. v. Texas point reinforces my hesitation to treat changes in enforcement posture as the kind of legally cognizable “adverse effect” that opens the courthouse doors in a way Congress did not clearly authorize.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that “any person adversely affected” is broad and that Congress elsewhere used “holder” language, but textualism requires reading those words in their statutory setting, including § 387l(a)(1)’s venue tether to the petitioner’s residence/principal place of business. As Chief Justice Roberts notes, National Ass’n of Manufacturers teaches that “any” does not nullify the limiting work done by accompanying channeling and venue terms; if downstream sellers can join solely to anchor venue, the venue limitation becomes largely self-defeating. The better original public meaning of “adversely affected” here is a legally cognizable effect from an order directed to the PMTA applicant, not derivative economic fallout or a shift in enforcement risk for retailers who lacked a lawful entitlement to sell the unauthorized product before and after the MDO. Justice Alito’s reference to United States v. Texas reinforces the caution against converting changes in enforcement likelihood into a statutory ticket to preferred judicial review in a way that destabilizes Congress’s review-and-venue design.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s textual argument about “any person adversely affected” is powerful, and I agree we must not rewrite “any.” But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the key statutory work is done by “adversely affected” within a channeling-and-venue scheme that would become administratively unmanageable if downstream retailers could join solely to manufacture a preferred circuit—an outcome in tension with Congress’s evident desire to cabin forum selection, consistent with National Ass’n of Manufacturers. I also find Justice Alito’s reliance on United States v. Texas probative in highlighting the danger of treating downstream economic fallout and enforcement-risk shifts as the kind of statutorily cognizable “adverse effect” that opens the courthouse doors and destabilizes the allocation of enforcement discretion.
